passages.speaker: Yaksha (Dharma in disguise)
events: Yudhishthira answers questions about dharma
He refuses water until he is permitted to answer for his brothers
passages.summary: A voice from a lake asks Yudhishthira a series of direct questions — what makes a man rich, what makes him kind, what makes him honoured — and accepts only answers that are true and useful. When Yudhishthira asks for water for his dying brothers, he is told to answer first. He does, and adds that he will not take what he has not earned the right to take, even while his brothers are dying.
passages.source_reference: Vana Parva — Aranya Parva, the Yaksha's questions (Yaksha Prashna)
passages.verification_note: Episode identity and parva location verified against the standard 18-parva division. `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.speaker: Markandeya narrating
events: Savitri chooses a husband who is fated to die
She follows Yama and wins back his life
passages.summary: Savitri is warned that the man she has chosen will die within a year and chooses him anyway. When death comes she follows it, and by refusing to leave — and by speaking well — she extracts first his sight, then his kingdom, then offspring, then his life. The story does not deny the loss; it shows attention, persistence and exact speech being converted into what looks like a reprieve.
passages.source_reference: Vana Parva — Aranya Parva, Savitri and Satyavan
passages.verification_note: Episode identity and parva location verified against the standard 18-parva division. `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.speaker: narrator
events: Nala gambles away his kingdom
Nala abandons Damayanti in the forest
Nala works as a cook in another king's household
passages.summary: A capable and beloved king loses his kingdom at dice, then loses himself: he abandons his sleeping wife in the forest and later serves in another man's kitchen under a false name. The story mirrors Yudhishthira's own fall and makes the same point about how gambling dissolves judgement in small, consecutive steps.
passages.source_reference: Vana Parva — Aranya Parva, Nala and Damayanti

passages.section: Aranya Parva — Draupadi's demand for vengeance
passages.speaker: Draupadi
events: Draupadi is abducted by Jayadratha
Krishna reassures her and arranges her rescue
passages.summary: Having waited years for redress, Draupadi tells Krishna directly that she will not tie her hair until it is washed in the blood of the men responsible. Krishna does not tell her to let it go; he acknowledges the claim and works toward it. The passage is evidence that the text sometimes endorses the demand for accountability rather than forbidding it.
passages.source_reference: Vana Parva — Aranya Parva, Draupadi after the abduction by Jayadratha

passages.section: Aranya Parva — Vidura visits the exiles
passages.speaker: Vidura
events: Vidura brings news and counsel
He urges the Pandavas to consider settlement and safety
passages.summary: Vidura comes to the forest camp carrying both news and advice. He tells Yudhishthira where responsibility for the disaster actually lies, and presses restraint where his listeners want permission to act. His loyalty does not require him to tell them what they want to hear.
passages.source_reference: Vana Parva — Aranya Parva, Vidura's visit to the Pandavas in exile

passages.section: Aranya Parva — Arjuna's penance and the fight with Shiva
passages.speaker: Shiva / Arjuna
events: Arjuna performs austerities
Arjuna fights a hunter (Shiva) and loses his bow
passages.summary: Arjuna undertakes austerities to gain a weapon sufficient for the war. In the forest he meets a hunter who contests his claim to the ground and the game; Arjuna loses, and only afterwards learns who it was. The episode removes any lingering idea that readiness is something you can simply demand.
passages.source_reference: Vana Parva — Aranya Parva, Arjuna's penance and the encounter with Shiva

passages.speaker: Markandeya
events: Yudhishthira asks why the just suffer
Markandeya tells stories in reply
passages.summary: Yudhishthira asks the plain question: why does a just man come to grief? Markandeya does not answer with a rule; he answers with stories, each of which shows suffering arriving through a different route. The text's method is to widen the question rather than close it.
passages.source_reference: Vana Parva — Aranya Parva, Markandeya's consolations

passages.speaker: narrator
events: Janamejaya begins a serpent sacrifice
Astika stops the sacrifice
passages.summary: Grieving his father, a king begins a sacrifice that will annihilate every serpent on earth. It is stopped only because a boy with a claim on him asks him to stop, mid-action, when the work is nearly done. The passage is about a grievance that has outgrown its reason and is halted by a relationship rather than by an argument.
passages.source_reference: Adi Parva — the snake sacrifice of Janamejaya and Astika's intervention
passages.verification_note: Episode identity and parva location verified; this event opens the epic's frame narrative in the Adi Parva. `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.speaker: Draupadi / Keechaka
events: Draupadi hides as a maidservant
Keechaka harasses her and is killed by Bhima
passages.summary: In hiding, Draupadi works in the queen's household and is cornered by a powerful courtier. She complains to the queen, then to the king, and is refused because he fears Keechaka's alliance. She then tells Bhima. The sequence shows what it costs to seek redress through channels that are not designed to give it.
passages.source_reference: Virata Parva — Sairishakh Parva, Draupadi and Keechaka

passages.section: Sairishakh Parva — the year in disguise
passages.speaker: narrator
events: Each Pandava takes a role suited to his skill
The identity is concealed for twelve months
passages.summary: To complete the thirteenth year undetected, each of the five takes a role that conceals rather than flatters him: the best archer teaches dance, the strongest becomes a cook. The discipline required is not combat but the willingness to be small in public for a long time.
passages.source_reference: Virata Parva — the year of hiding in Matsya

passages.section: Sairishakh Parva — the recovery of the cattle
passages.speaker: Arjuna / Uttara
events: The Kaurava army takes Virata's cattle
Arjuna fights alone behind a single chariot
passages.summary: A prince is asked to ride out against the army that has taken the kingdom's herds and discovers he cannot. Arjuna takes the reins behind him, names every commander opposing them, and sends the prince back to fetch help. The scene is a compact study in fear being met by someone whose competence makes the same fear manageable.
passages.source_reference: Virata Parva — Sairishakh Parva, the recovery of the cattle
